The bulls could cling to something worthy while they watch semiconductor stocks such as Sandisk ( [SNDK](https://finance.yahoo.com/quote/SNDK/)) and Micron ( [MU](https://finance.yahoo.com/quote/MU/)) get blown to pieces.

About 72% of S&P 500 stocks are now trading above their 200-day moving average, the strongest market breadth since December 2024, according to data from Barchart (see below). The benchmark index is also holding near record highs.

[![A win for the bulls.](<Base64-Image-Removed>)](https://s.yimg.com/lo/mysterio/api/afb08dd185e7206a408a0aeef2b335d25a38982dc6648d640daaa9c25a39d532/lightyear_networkapi/resizefit_w960%3Bquality_80%3Bformat_webp/https%3A%2F%2Fd29szjachogqwa.cloudfront.net%2Fimages%2Fuser-uploaded%2Fhoxlr0oweaewscj_2088.jpeg)

A win for the bulls.·Barchart

"You've got essentially two-thirds of S&P 500 companies that are trading above their 200-day moving average. That's relatively healthy and still consistent with the market that is more rotational in nature and not necessarily one that is correctional," Charles Schwab strategist Kevin Gordon said on [Yahoo Finance's Opening Bid](https://finance.yahoo.com/videos/series/opening-bid/).

Investors have cashed in their AI bets and have rotated into software, financials, industrials, healthcare, and consumer discretionary stocks for their perceived values. A strong earnings season from many companies, like Coca-Cola ( [KO](https://finance.yahoo.com/quote/KO/)) on Tuesday, has helped offset the negative tones stemming from reports out of Alphabet ( [GOOGL](https://finance.yahoo.com/quote/GOOGL/)) and Tesla ( [TSLA](https://finance.yahoo.com/quote/TSLA/)).

The market has also been supported by resilient economic data, continued expectations for Federal Reserve rate cuts over the next year, and robust corporate profit growth, all of which have kept money flowing into stocks.

In addition, the S&P 500's diversified makeup means gains in companies outside of semiconductors — including software firms, internet platforms, banks, and retailers — have cushioned the impact of declines in Nvidia ( [NVDA](https://finance.yahoo.com/quote/NVDA/)), AMD ( [AMD](https://finance.yahoo.com/quote/AMD/)), Broadcom ( [AVGO](https://finance.yahoo.com/quote/AVGO/)), and other chipmakers.

Ultimately, investors increasingly view the semiconductor summer rout as a repricing of AI infrastructure expectations rather than a signal that the broader US economy or corporate earnings outlook is poised to fall off a cliff.

Gordon said, " I don't necessarily take a negative economic message from it \[the chip sell-off\]. From a GDP side of things, I don't necessarily think that the sell off you can directly attribute it to what's going to happen sort of in the economy."

The list is re-evaluated on a recurring basis against primary sources, including 10-K and 10-Q filings, earnings press releases, and company disclosures, to confirm what each business actually does in semiconductors today.

### Categories of semiconductor stocks

The companies on this list fall into several sub-segments of the semiconductor value chain:

- **Chipmakers (logic, CPU, and GPU):** firms that design and sell processors and accelerators, such as NVDA, AMD, INTC, QCOM, CBRS, and AMBA.
- **Foundries:** contract manufacturers that fabricate chips designed by others, such as TSM, GFS, UMC, and TSEM.
- **Equipment:** makers of the tools used to build chips, including lithography, etch, deposition, test, and metrology, such as ASML, AMAT, LRCX, KLAC, TER, KLIC, and VECO.
- **Memory and storage:** producers of DRAM, NAND flash, storage controllers, and memory-interface chips, such as MU, SNDK, SIMO, and RMBS.
- **Analog and power:** suppliers of analog, mixed-signal, microcontroller, and power-management chips, such as TXN, ADI, MCHP, ON, MPWR, POWI, DIOD, and ALGM.
- **RF and connectivity:** designers of radio-frequency and high-speed interconnect chips, such as SWKS, QRVO, MRVL, CRDO, ALAB, and SMTC.
- **EDA and IP:** software and intellectual-property vendors used to design chips, such as SNPS, CDNS, and ARM.
- **Materials, specialty, and packaging:** materials and photomask suppliers, wide-bandgap device makers, programmable logic, and assembly and test providers, such as ENTG, PLAB, WOLF, LSCC, ASX, and AMKR.

### What moves semiconductor stocks

Semiconductor companies are sensitive to several common factors. Demand cycles for personal computers, smartphones, data-center hardware, automotive electronics, and industrial equipment can shift order volumes. Capital spending plans from chipmakers and foundries affect equipment and materials suppliers. Inventory levels across the supply chain, pricing for memory and other commodity-like products, and the pace of new process-node adoption also play a role. Trade policy, export controls, and supply-chain conditions can affect where and how chips are produced and sold.

### Risks and considerations

The semiconductor industry is cyclical, and revenue and margins can swing with demand cycles and inventory corrections. The business is capital-intensive, and building or upgrading fabrication plants requires large, long-lead spending that may not align with near-term demand. The sector is exposed to geopolitics, including export controls, tariffs, and concentration of advanced manufacturing in specific regions. Individual companies also face competition, customer concentration, technology-transition, and supply-chain risks. The presence of a company on this list does not imply any view about its prospects.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### What are semiconductor stocks?

Semiconductor stocks are shares of companies that design, manufacture, or supply the chips and tools used in electronics. The group includes chip designers, contract foundries, and the makers of the equipment, materials, and software used to produce chips. These chips power computers, smartphones, data centers, cars, and industrial and networking hardware.

### What types of companies are included in this semiconductor list?

The list spans several sub-segments of the semiconductor value chain: chipmakers that design logic, CPU, and GPU products; foundries that fabricate chips; equipment and materials suppliers; memory producers; analog and power chip makers; radio-frequency and connectivity designers; electronic-design-automation and intellectual-property vendors; and specialty and packaging companies.

### How are the companies on this page selected and ordered?

This page collects US-listed companies whose business is centered on, or materially tied to, the semiconductor industry. Each company receives an affinity score that reflects how central semiconductors are to its business, and the list is ordered by that score and then by market capitalization. The page is for informational purposes only and is not investment advice.

### What risks affect semiconductor stocks?

Semiconductor companies are exposed to a cyclical, capital-intensive industry where demand cycles, inventory corrections, and pricing for products such as memory can affect results. The sector is also sensitive to trade policy and export controls, regional concentration of advanced manufacturing, technology transitions, competition, and supply-chain conditions.

### How is this list of semiconductor stocks maintained?

The list is reviewed on a recurring basis against primary sources, including annual and quarterly filings, earnings releases, and company disclosures. A company is added only when its semiconductor role is documented, either through disclosed semiconductor revenue or a verifiable position in the chip supply chain, and companies that publish heavy semiconductor language while reporting no semiconductor revenue are screened out. Companies are removed when the case weakens, for example financial distress, an agreed acquisition or going-private transaction, or a divested semiconductor business.

### What is the difference between a fabless chip company, a foundry, and an integrated device manufacturer?

A fabless company designs chips and pays someone else to build them, which is how Nvidia, AMD, and Qualcomm operate. A foundry manufactures chips that other companies design, and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing, GlobalFoundries, and United Microelectronics work this way. An integrated device manufacturer designs and fabricates its own chips in its own plants, which describes Texas Instruments, Micron, and Intel. Intel also sells foundry services to outside customers, so a single company can sit in more than one category.
